standard.title: Data as objects and symbols
standard.description: represent data as objects, pictures and symbols
standard.prior_knowledge: This is the first data representation descriptor in the curriculum. Students have no prior DT knowledge assumed. They bring general experience matching pictures to real things and using symbols in everyday life (e.g. toilet signs, traffic lights). They have not yet used the word 'data' or connected representation to the idea that a symbol or picture stands in for information.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent data using objects, pictures and symbols, and understand that the representation stands in for the data — it is not the data itself.

nodes.label: Representing data as pictures and objects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use pictures or objects to represent data about themselves or their environment
nodes.minimum_width: Use a picture or object to represent one piece of data about themselves or a classmate (e.g. draw a picture representing a family member's interest)
nodes.typical_width: Represent data about multiple people or things using pictures or objects across at least two contexts (e.g. draw family members with their interests; use coloured blocks to represent students' sports houses)
wider: Draw pictures representing each family member and their interests — explain what each picture represents and why that picture was chosen
Use coloured blocks to represent an attribute of the class (e.g. sports houses, favourite animals) — explain what each colour or block stands for

response_modes.reason: Accurate representation requires students to make and hold a deliberate correspondence between a picture/object and the data it represents. Foundation students need repeated practice making these correspondences across different data types before the abstract concept of representation (the picture is not the thing, it stands for the thing) can be addressed.

success_criteria: Produces a picture or object that represents a specific piece of data
Can say what the picture or object represents when asked
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not established accurate picture-to-data correspondences cannot attempt Node 2's conceptual move — that a symbol is not the data itself requires a working model of representation to interrogate.

nodes.label: Recognising that a symbol is not the data itself
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify symbols that represent ideas or data, and understand that the symbol is not the data itself
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one symbol that represents an idea; explain what the symbol means and that the symbol itself is not the thing it represents
nodes.typical_width: Identify multiple symbols representing ideas in familiar contexts (flags, road signs, app icons, weather symbols); explain what each symbol represents; discuss that the symbol is a stand-in for the idea, not the idea itself
wider: Examine the symbols and colours on the Australian Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag — identify what each element represents and discuss why symbols are used to represent important ideas
Compare an app icon on a screen with what the app does — explain that the icon is a symbol representing the app, not the app itself

response_modes.reason: The conceptual shift — that a symbol is not the data itself — is the hardest idea in this descriptor. Students readily accept that a picture of a dog represents a dog, but struggle with the arbitrariness of symbols (why does a red octagon mean stop?). Multiple symbol contexts, especially culturally significant ones like flags, help students see that the symbol-meaning relationship is constructed and intentional.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The flag direction is genuinely rich — the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags are culturally significant symbols where each element carries deliberate meaning. This makes the symbol/data distinction substantive and culturally situated rather than purely abstract.
success_criteria: Names at least one symbol and states what it represents
Explains (in simple terms) that the symbol is not the same as the thing it stands for
